lessons.description: Learn written authorization, scope boundaries, safe methods, evidence handling and reporting. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 1 — Ethics, permission, scope and rules of engagement

LEARNING OUTCOME
Learn written authorization, scope boundaries, safe methods, evidence handling and reporting.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Permission comes first

Ethical hacking is a controlled assessment performed for a system owner under explicit authorization. Curiosity, a public IP address, an exposed login page or a person’s employer is not permission. Before testing, obtain written authorization, identify exact targets and dates, list allowed and prohibited actions, agree on data handling and document a stop condition.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Written permission. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Scope boundary. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Define scope

A useful scope states assets, testing windows, test accounts, data limits, rate limits, third-party boundaries and reporting contacts. Never expand to a related domain, another tenant or a personal account because it appears connected. If scope is unclear, stop and request clarification.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Safety guardrail. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Data handling. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Protect people and systems

Use synthetic data, avoid collecting credentials, do not attempt persistence or destructive actions, redact evidence and notify the owner if a serious issue or accidental exposure appears. Never try to obtain private information about a suspected person.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Stop conditions. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Report path. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Guided practice — learn by doing

Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.output: Written scope is the boundary that tells a tester when to stop.

blocks.text: Lesson 2 — Build a safe Linux and virtual lab

LEARNING OUTCOME
Prepare an isolated practice setup with snapshots, test accounts and controlled targets.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Keep the lab separate

Use a virtual machine or deliberately vulnerable training app. Prefer a host-only or isolated virtual network, non-sensitive test accounts, snapshots and disposable data. Do not connect a vulnerable lab directly to a work or home network unless the exposure is intentional and controlled.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Host system. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Isolated VM. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Learn local Linux safely

Commands such as `pwd`, `whoami`, `ip addr`, `ss -tulpen`, `ls -la` and `man` help inspect your own environment. Learn paths and permissions. Do not run unknown scripts with administrator privileges or paste secrets into shell history.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Private network. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Snapshot. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Reset and document

Create a snapshot before experiments. Record lab version and time. If behavior is unexpected, stop and restore the snapshot instead of escalating privileges or trying the same action against a live target.

Visual 6/6 — Clean shutdown. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Lesson 3 — Passive reconnaissance and approved asset context

LEARNING OUTCOME
Gather non-invasive information from approved technical documentation without profiling private people.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Passive still has limits

Use provided documentation, a fictional inventory, approved public technical documentation and facts supplied by the owner. Avoid collecting information about private individuals or combining personal details into a profile. The goal is to define permitted assets and exposures, not target a person.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Approved scope. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Public documentation. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Check source quality

Record where a fact came from, when it was observed, and whether it is verified or inferred. An old domain record may be stale; a software name does not prove a vulnerable version. Ask the owner to confirm asset ownership before active assessment.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Asset inventory. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Source confidence. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Build an asset register
Record asset ID, owner, environment, service purpose, data class, written permission and expiry date. Use fake hostnames in exercises and keep the register in an approved workspace.

Visual 6/6 — Evidence log. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Lesson 4 — Network discovery inside your own lab

LEARNING OUTCOME
Understand hosts, ports, services and observations in a private, authorized practice environment.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Know the terms

A host is a device or virtual system; a port is a logical service endpoint; a service is the application listening there. A discovery result is an observation, not proof of a weakness. Compare observations with the documented design and authorized scope.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Lab host. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Port concept. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Use the provided lab target

Use the exact private target supplied in your course lab, not an arbitrary public address. Begin with the lab checklist and tool documentation. Keep intensity within the rules of engagement and save only the output needed for the report.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Service inventory. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Version context. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Make a finding actionable
Record target ID, service, expected and observed behavior, timestamp, evidence reference, impact, confidence and follow-up. If a host is outside scope, do not test it further.

blocks.text: Lesson 5 — Vulnerability assessment and risk prioritization

LEARNING OUTCOME
Validate scanner output, identify false positives, estimate impact and recommend fixes.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Treat output as a hypothesis

Tools may flag outdated versions or settings, but findings can be false positives or duplicate symptoms. Validate asset identity, version source, configuration and patch status safely. Do not use intrusive proof-of-concept code just to make a scanner result look important.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Scanner output. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Validate evidence. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Prioritize using context

Consider exposure, privileges required, business criticality, data sensitivity, compensating controls and evidence that a vulnerability is exploited. CVSS helps describe technical severity but does not fully represent business risk. Use the owner’s model and current advisories to set remediation order.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — False positives. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Impact estimate. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Give a useful fix

Include safe reproduction steps, expected and observed behavior, impact, affected configuration, mitigation and retest criteria. Redact personal data and secrets; reports belong only in approved channels.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Priority order. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Remediation. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.text: Lesson 6 — Web security testing with training applications

LEARNING OUTCOME
Assess input handling, authorization and sessions only in deliberately vulnerable training apps.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Use a purpose-built target

Practice in OWASP Juice Shop or an authorized PortSwigger lab. Learn how requests, responses, cookies, tokens and APIs work. Keep the browser, proxy and target limited to that training environment. Do not test real company sites or accounts without written permission.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Browser request. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Training target. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Test the defense, not a person

Check whether the server validates data, verifies access for each record and protects session state. Use provided lab accounts and synthetic records. A successful login is not permission to read someone else’s information.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Authorization check. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Input boundary. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Explain and fix the cause

Use server-side authorization, parameterized database queries, context-aware output encoding, secure session settings and safe error handling. After a fix in your sample app, repeat the same lab check and show that the prohibited behavior is rejected.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Safe evidence. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Verified fix. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

lessons.title: Password controls, hashing, MFA and account safety
lessons.subtitle: Evaluate defensive password practices and account recovery without using real credentials.
lessons.description: Evaluate defensive password practices and account recovery without using real credentials. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 7 — Password controls, hashing, MFA and account safety

LEARNING OUTCOME
Evaluate defensive password practices and account recovery without using real credentials.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Protect the password lifecycle

Use unique credentials, MFA, rate limits and a recovery process that does not undermine login security. Administrators should never ask users to reveal their password or one-time code. If credentials are exposed, reset through the approved process, revoke sessions and review logs.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Password policy. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Salted hash. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Hashing is not reversible encryption

A password verifier uses a password-specific hashing scheme, unique salt and suitable work parameters. A salt is not a secret; it prevents identical passwords from producing identical stored hashes. Do not invent a hashing algorithm or store raw passwords. Use only synthetic sample data.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — MFA factors. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Recovery flow. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Strengthen the whole account

MFA, passkeys, device and session management, abuse-resistant recovery and sign-in alerts provide defense in depth. Rate limits should resist guessing without making denial of service easy. Monitoring unusual sign-ins and unexpected MFA prompts helps defenders detect account abuse.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Rate limit. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Account review. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.text: Lesson 8 — Safe proof-of-concept thinking and remediation

LEARNING OUTCOME
Use minimal toy examples to explain a weakness, patch it, and prove the correction.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Keep the demonstration minimal

A proof of concept demonstrates one hypothesis safely in a toy app or intentionally vulnerable lab. Use synthetic input and the smallest action needed. Avoid persistence, stealth, data extraction, destructive behavior or code aimed at anything outside the lab.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Hypothesis. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Toy input. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Connect weakness to control

A sample form might fail to validate a value against an allow-list. Show the expected input, validation rule and failing test using fabricated data. Fix it with server-side validation and regression tests. The lesson is complete when the same test is rejected after the fix.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Minimal evidence. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Patch. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Document cleanup

Record lab target, authorization reference, test data, timestamp, step and outcome. Remove test files or temporary accounts created within scope. If anything crosses the boundary, stop and notify the owner rather than hiding it.

blocks.caption: Visual 5/6 — Regression test. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 6/6 — Scope note. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Guided practice — learn by doing

Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.text: Lesson 9 — Evidence, severity, disclosure and professional reports

LEARNING OUTCOME
Write reproducible findings with evidence, impact, remediation and safe retest steps.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Structure the report

A finding includes a clear title, affected asset, severity rationale, confidence, business impact, prerequisites, safe reproduction, evidence reference, remediation and retest checklist. Report what evidence proves; do not infer who is responsible from one log entry or IP address.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Finding anatomy. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Reproduction steps. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Handle evidence as sensitive

Collect the minimum needed, preserve timestamps, restrict access and redact secrets and personal data. Never publish scan output or screenshots online. Follow the owner’s retention and deletion process.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Impact. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Evidence. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Disclose responsibly

Use the designated contact or disclosure channel, agree on timelines and avoid threatening public disclosure. Retest only within the authorized scope and mark the issue fixed, partially fixed or unresolved.

blocks.text: Lesson 10 — Authorized assessment capstone and retest

LEARNING OUTCOME
Plan a bounded lab assessment, test safely, report findings and retest fixes.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.
1. Plan the work

Use a fictional organization or approved training target. Prepare written authorization, exact scope, testing hours, safety limits, data rules and emergency contact. Define success criteria before testing.

blocks.caption: Visual 1/6 — Authorization. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 2/6 — Assessment plan. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 2. Perform a controlled review

Follow lab instructions, record observations, validate only what the target permits and avoid actions affecting other users. Rank findings by evidence and impact. Recommend specific controls like authorization checks, input validation, session handling, dependency updates or defensive configuration.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Lab run. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Report. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: 3. Close the loop

Deliver the agreed scope, asset list, finding log, remediation plan, retest evidence and lessons learned. Communicate serious issues promptly through the approved contact. A professional result is a safer system and a clear report, not unauthorized access.
